quests.instruction: Choose the sentence that gives evidence for the claim, not just another opinion.
quests.prompt: Claim: Language-learning apps help beginners learn faster.
options: Learning a language is much easier when the lessons are fun and short, which is why so many people prefer apps.
Beginners who try an app before they sign up for any course usually find it a cheap and friendly way to start.
In our class trial, the 12 students who used the app daily scored higher on the vocabulary test than the 14 who did not.
Apps are a wonderful modern way for students to learn a new language, and they fit easily into a busy day.
quests.hint: Evidence is something that happened or was measured. An opinion only says what someone thinks.
quests.explanation: The trial result is a measured comparison. The other sentences are opinions or advice that would need evidence themselves.

quests.instruction: Which sentence is evidence for the claim?
quests.prompt: Claim: Open-plan offices make communication easier.
options: Communication is the key to a successful company in any industry.
Our survey found that 41 of 60 staff spoke to colleagues more often after the move.
Everyone should be able to talk freely at work with anyone else.
Open spaces feel friendly, modern and welcoming to most visitors.
quests.hint: Look for something counted or observed rather than valued.
quests.explanation: The survey figures show a change in behaviour. The other sentences state beliefs about communication and open spaces.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO sentences that give evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: Summer jobs help teenagers become more responsible.
options: A school survey of 200 former students found that those with summer jobs missed fewer deadlines in college.
My neighbour's son began arriving on time and saving money after his first summer job.
Teenagers should think carefully about their futures before choosing a job.
Responsibility is an important quality for teenagers to develop early.
quests.hint: Which sentences report something that actually happened?
quests.explanation: A survey result and a real example both show what happened. The other two are general statements of opinion.

quests.instruction: Which sentence uses a statistic (a number from counting or measuring)?
quests.prompt: Claim: Reading on the train is popular with commuters.
options: The city's transport manager believes reading is popular among most passengers.
My neighbour reads a novel on the train every single morning.
Reading on the train is a lovely way to pass the time on a long journey.
Nearly three out of four commuters in the survey said they read on the train.
quests.hint: A statistic shows how many or how much, usually from a survey or count.
quests.explanation: 'Three out of four' is a figure taken from a survey. The other options are a personal example, an opinion and a manager's belief.

quests.instruction: Which sentence uses an expert or official source as evidence?
quests.prompt: Claim: Skipping breakfast can affect students' concentration.
options: I skipped breakfast once and felt dizzy during a maths lesson on Friday.
According to the school nurse, students who skip breakfast often feel dizzy by the second lesson.
Breakfast is essential for every student who wants to learn well.
In the school survey, 40 percent of students said that they skip breakfast.
quests.hint: Look for a named person with relevant knowledge.
quests.explanation: The school nurse is a knowledgeable source reporting what she sees. The remaining options are a survey figure, a personal experience and a general opinion.

quests.instruction: Which sentence is a personal example?
quests.prompt: Claim: Using a paper planner helps people meet deadlines.
options: A time-management coach advises planning the next day the night before.
When I started using a paper planner last spring, I stopped missing my deadlines.
In a poll of 500 workers, 62 percent said that they use a planner every week.
Planners are the best way to stay organised in a busy job or school.
quests.hint: A personal example comes from the writer's own experience.
quests.explanation: The first sentence describes what happened to the writer. The remaining options are a poll result, an expert's advice and an opinion.

quests.instruction: Choose the evidence that is relevant to the claim.
quests.prompt: Claim: The town should lower the speed limit outside schools.
options: After the limit was lowered outside Oak Primary, reported near-misses dropped from nine to two in a year.
The road outside the school is about 300 metres long and has a bus stop at each end of the block.
Cars have become more powerful over the last several decades, and many drivers now travel faster than before.
Oak Primary has around 400 pupils and 25 teachers, and many of the pupils walk to school each morning.
quests.hint: Ask which fact shows what a lower limit actually did.
quests.explanation: Fewer near-misses after a lower limit directly links the change to safety. The other facts are about the school, the road or cars in general.

quests.instruction: Choose the relevant evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: Our bakery should sell more vegan products.
options: Our bakery opens at six every morning and closes at four.
Vegan food is often discussed in magazines and on television.
Every week we turn away about twenty customers who ask for vegan options.
The bakery sells bread, pastries, cakes and several kinds of biscuits.
quests.hint: The evidence should show customer demand for the product.
quests.explanation: Turned-away customers show real demand. The other statements describe the bakery or the general popularity of a topic.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO pieces of evidence that are relevant.
quests.prompt: Claim: The company should provide adjustable standing desks.
options: Twelve staff members reported back pain in last year's health survey.
The desks are delivered in flat boxes and put together on site.
On the pilot floor, staff with adjustable desks said they felt less stiff.
The company has 240 employees working across two different buildings.
quests.hint: Look for evidence about the problem or the effect of the desks.
quests.explanation: Back pain and improvement with adjustable desks connect to the claim. The company size and delivery details do not.

quests.instruction: Choose the most precise evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: The recycling scheme is working.
options: A lot less waste is going to landfill sites than there was before.
Household waste sent to landfill fell from 480 tonnes to 350 tonnes in six months.
The amount of rubbish has changed in a noticeable way recently.
People seem to be much happier about recycling these days.
quests.hint: Precise evidence has numbers, dates or clear comparisons.
quests.explanation: The best sentence gives exact amounts and a time period. The rest say 'a lot' and 'noticeable' without any figure.

quests.instruction: Choose the most precise evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: The customer service line has poor response times.
options: I waited a very long time on the phone before anyone answered me.
Between 9 and 11 a.m. last Monday, I waited 47 minutes and was cut off twice.
Lots of other customers have had the same problem as I have.
Calls always seem to take much longer than they should really take.
quests.hint: Which version could be checked against a call record?
quests.explanation: Time, length of wait and number of disconnections give exact details. The other sentences only express frustration in general terms.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision of the vague sentence.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Many students walk to school.'
options: Quite a lot of students walk to school every single day.
A big number of students seem to prefer walking there.
In a class survey, 22 of 30 students walk to school.
Most students probably walk or cycle to their school.
quests.hint: A better version says who was asked and how many.
quests.explanation: The revision names the source and gives a count. The rest still use vague phrases like 'quite a lot' or 'probably'.

quests.instruction: Which claim does this evidence actually support?
quests.prompt: Evidence: Ana tried the new bus route once and arrived early.
options: The new route was faster for Ana on that trip.
Buses on the new route are more reliable than the trains in town.
The new bus route is faster for all of the passengers who use it.
The new route will be quicker than the old one every day of the week.
quests.hint: One trip can show only what happened on that trip.
quests.explanation: A single journey supports only a claim about that journey. The other claims need many trips or many people.

quests.instruction: Choose the evidence that is enough to support the claim.
quests.prompt: Claim: Most students in our year prefer online tests.
options: In a poll of 120 of the 150 students in our year, 84 chose online tests.
Two of my friends have told me that they prefer online tests to paper ones.
One student wrote a long complaint about the paper tests last week.
The teacher mentioned that online tests will be introduced next term.
quests.hint: A claim about 'most students' needs a large, well-chosen sample.
quests.explanation: A poll covering most of the year group with a clear majority supports 'most'. The other options are opinions from very few people or a fact about scheduling.

quests.instruction: Choose the addition that would make the evidence sufficient.
quests.prompt: Claim: Customers love the new app. Current evidence: three people gave it five stars on Friday.
options: The app was released to the public at the start of March.
In the store's rating list, 1,400 of 1,800 reviews give it four or five stars.
Five stars is the highest rating that a customer can give on the app.
One reviewer said that the app was very easy to use and clear.
quests.hint: You need evidence from many customers, not a few.
quests.explanation: A high share of a large number of reviews supports a claim about customers in general. The other options add no scale.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: Cooking classes help teenagers eat more healthily.
options: A friend of mine took a cooking class last term and enjoyed it so much that she signed up for another.
A famous chef says that learning to cook is the key to a healthy life and that everyone should try it.
Cooking classes are now held in many towns and cities across the country, often in the evenings and at weekends.
Six months after a school cooking course, 65 of the 80 participants were making a meal from scratch each week.
quests.hint: Strong evidence is measured, connected to the claim and not just praise or fame.
quests.explanation: The follow-up figures show a change in habits after the course. The rest are enjoyment, availability and a celebrity's opinion.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: Reminder texts reduce missed appointments.
options: At the clinic, missed appointments fell from 18% to 9% after reminder texts began.
Text messages are read within minutes by most people who receive them.
Reminders are sent by many businesses as part of normal service.
I forgot an appointment once when I did not receive a reminder message.
quests.hint: Look for a before-and-after comparison.
quests.explanation: The clinic's drop shows what changed after the texts. The other options are one story, a general fact and a common practice.

quests.instruction: Select the TWO strongest pieces of evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: A breakfast club improves school attendance.
options: Breakfast clubs are very popular with parents who work early shifts.
Breakfast is often described as the most important meal of the day.
After the breakfast club opened, average attendance rose from 91% to 95%.
Teachers noticed that students who attended the club were rarely late.
quests.hint: Choose the evidence connected directly to attendance.
quests.explanation: Attendance rates and teachers' observations link the club to attendance. Popularity with parents and slogans about breakfast do not.

quests.instruction: Choose the most reliable source.
quests.prompt: Claim: The local tap water is safe to drink.
options: An advertisement for a brand of bottled water in the newspaper.
The city water authority's published test results for this month.
A post from an anonymous user on an online forum last week.
Something my neighbour heard from a friend at the gym.
quests.hint: A reliable source has expertise, records and no reason to benefit from the answer.
quests.explanation: Published test results are checked and public. The other choices are anonymous, second-hand or advertising with a motive.

quests.instruction: Choose the most reliable evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: A new phone's battery lasts longer than older models.
options: A single customer's comment on an online shopping page.
The manufacturer's advertising slogan about all-day power.
An independent test that ran ten phones through the same battery task.
A rumour that was shared in a friends' group chat.
quests.hint: Which source treated all the phones equally and has no reason to favour one?
quests.explanation: A fair, independent test gives comparable results. Advertising, one comment and rumour are less reliable.

quests.instruction: Which evidence should a reader treat with the most caution?
quests.prompt: Claim: Membership at Peak Gym makes people fitter.
options: Peak Gym's own advertisement saying its members are the fittest people in town.
A health survey of 3,000 adults run by a university department, comparing gym members with other adults.
Fitness test records reviewed by the local hospital, covering members and non-members over several years.
A report by an independent consumer organisation that compared the fitness of gym members across the country.
quests.hint: Ask who is making the statement and what they gain.
quests.explanation: A business promoting itself has a reason to exaggerate. Independent researchers and health services have less reason to favour the gym.

quests.instruction: Which claim does the evidence actually support?
quests.prompt: Evidence: Ten students in Class 6 said Thursday's homework kept them up late.
options: Some Class 6 students found Thursday's homework too heavy.
All children in the country have far too much homework every night.
Homework should be banned in every primary school in the town.
Homework harms children's health and should be stopped.
quests.hint: Match the size of the claim to the size of the evidence.
quests.explanation: The evidence covers one class and one night. The other claims cover all children, all nights or all schools.

quests.instruction: The evidence proves only part of the claim. Which part?
quests.prompt: Claim: Electric scooters are cheap, safe and fast. Evidence: A test showed a scooter trip across town took 12 minutes, compared with 25 by bus.
options: That they are safe for both riders and walkers.
That they are cheap to own and to run.
That they can be fast.
That they are better than buses in every way.
quests.hint: Read the evidence carefully and ask what it measures.
quests.explanation: The test measured journey time only. It says nothing about cost or safety, and it does not compare every quality.

quests.instruction: Choose the claim the evidence is strong enough to support.
quests.prompt: Evidence: In our school, 18 of 20 students who joined the reading club improved their test scores.
options: Reading is the most effective way to improve test results.
Most students in our school's reading club improved their scores.
Reading clubs raise the test scores of every student who joins them.
Every school in the country should set up a reading club.
quests.hint: The safest claim describes only the group that was measured.
quests.explanation: This claim matches the group in the evidence. The rest generalise to all students, all methods or all schools.

quests.instruction: What is missing from this evidence?
quests.prompt: Claim: The new parking rules are unfair to workers. Evidence: Parking now costs £8 a day.
options: The colour of the signs that show the new parking rules.
The name of the company that manages the car park.
How the cost compares with the old price or with workers' pay.
How many cars can be parked on one street at a time.
quests.hint: A single number needs something to compare it with.
quests.explanation: £8 means little without a comparison. The other missing details would not help judge whether the rules are unfair.

quests.instruction: What is missing?
quests.prompt: Claim: Students who eat lunch outside concentrate better. Evidence: Students in Class 4 who ate lunch outside scored 8 out of 10 on the afternoon quiz.
options: The number of desks in each classroom in Class 4.
How long the lunch break lasts at other schools.
The name of the person who wrote the quiz questions.
The scores of students who ate lunch inside.
quests.hint: To say something is 'better', you must compare it with something else.
quests.explanation: Without the comparison group, we cannot tell whether 8 out of 10 is high. The other details don't help compare the groups.

quests.instruction: Which extra information would best fill the gap in the evidence?
quests.prompt: Claim: Our customers want longer opening hours. Evidence: Two customers asked about it last week.
options: The year in which the shop was first opened to the public.
A photograph of the notice in the shop's front window.
How many customers asked over the past month, out of everyone who visited.
A list of the opening times of shops in nearby streets.
quests.hint: Two people is a small number. What would show how common the request is?
quests.explanation: A count out of all visitors shows how widespread the request is. The other options are related to the shop but say nothing about customers' wishes.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest evidence.
quests.prompt: Claim: A bag charge reduces plastic waste in our town.
options: Many shops now sell reusable bags near the checkout at reasonable prices.
I always carry a cloth bag with me when I go out to the shops.
Local supermarkets handed out 40% fewer plastic bags in the year after the charge began.
Plastic waste is a serious environmental issue for cities all over the world.
quests.hint: Look for a change that can be linked to the charge.
quests.explanation: A measured drop after the charge links the policy to fewer bags. The other options are general, personal or about sales.

quests.instruction: Which sentence should be replaced with more precise evidence?
quests.prompt: A paragraph says: 'Many staff use the new lift. Sixty-one of the 90 staff signed the petition. The lift was installed in June.'
options: Many staff use the new lift.
Sixty-one of the 90 staff signed the petition.
The lift was installed in June of this year.
The petition was signed by staff in both buildings.
quests.hint: Find the sentence with a vague quantity.
quests.explanation: 'Many staff' gives no count. The other sentences already contain exact numbers or details.

quests.instruction: Put the sentences in the best order: claim, evidence, detail, closing.
quests.prompt: Arrange the sentences about paper cups in an office kitchen.
options: That is roughly forty cups every working day.
Washable cups would remove most of this waste at little cost.
Last month we threw away about 900 paper cups.
Our office should switch to reusable cups in the kitchen.
quests.hint: The claim comes first, and the last sentence looks forward to the solution.
quests.explanation: The claim opens, the count gives evidence, the daily figure makes it easier to picture, and the closing links back to the claim.
